Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Louisiana Gov. Bobby Jindal is set to deliver the Republican response to President Obama's upcoming joint address to Congress, a high-profile slot the party often gives to one of its rising stars. Louisiana Gov. Bobby Jindal, 37, will give GOP response to President Obama's address to Congress this month. "Gov. Jindal embodies what I have long said: The Republican Party must not be simply the party of 'opposition,' but the party of better solutions," House Minority Leader John Boehner said in a Wednesday statement. Jindal, a former congressman in his first term as Louisiana's governor, was widely believed to be on Republican presidential nominee John McCain's short list for vice president, and he often served as a campaign surrogate on the Arizona senator's behalf. The 37-year-old son of Indian immigrants also was given a prime-time speaking slot at the GOP convention last September, though he ultimately decided not to attend the four-day event as Hurricane Gustav headed for landfall in his state. An Ivy League grad and Rhodes Scholar, and his state's first nonwhite governor, Jindal has long been on the GOP's radar screen as a potential future leader and likely presidential candidate. And as the GOP is launching full-scale efforts to appeal to nonwhite voters, Jindal has become one of the party's most high-profile minorities. "His stewardship of the state of Louisiana, dedication to reforming government and commitment to bringing forth new and innovative ideas make him a leader not just within the Republican Party, but in our nation as a whole," Boehner also said of Jindal on Wednesday. Jindal, who became governor two years after Hurricane Katrina ravaged Louisiana, has drawn praise for spearheading the ongoing recovery efforts. "When you look at major statewide offices Republicans have won over the past three years, there is one, Louisiana," said Alex Castellanos, a CNN contributor and Republican strategist. "In a state where we lost confidence in government, perhaps more than any other state, he restored it and cut taxes." Though he is often mentioned as a likely contender for the 2012 Republican presidential race, Jindal has said his current focus is on winning reelection in 2011. Jindal also said late last year that even if he were considering running for president, now is the time to support the sitting president. "It doesn't matter whether you're Republican, Democrat or independent, it doesn't matter whether you voted for him or not, President-elect Barack Obama is our president," he said. The White House announced on Tuesday that Obama will deliver the annual State of the Union address to both houses of Congress on February 24. In 2008, Democrats tapped Kansas Gov. Kathleen Sebelius -- then considered to be a possible vice presidential candidate -- to give the rebuttal speech to former President Bush's final State of the Union address. Other Democrats who delivered responses to Bush's State of the Unions include Virginia Sen. Jim Webb, Virginia Gov. Tim Kaine, and former Washington Gov. Gary Locke, the nation's first Chinese-American governor. The last Republican to deliver a response to a State of the Union address was Maine Sen. Susan Collins in 2000.

## GOP taps Bobby Jindal to answer Obama

Republican congressional leaders selected Louisiana Gov. Bobby Jindal to deliver the party’s televised response to President Barack Obama’s address to a joint session of Congress on Feb. 24, 2009. The choice elevated one of the GOP’s youngest and most prominent rising figures at a moment when the party was seeking a new identity after losing the White House and additional congressional seats in 2008.

House Republican leader John Boehner and Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell portrayed Jindal as an example of reform-minded, fiscally conservative leadership outside Washington. His selection also helped the party showcase greater generational and ethnic diversity opposite Obama, then the country’s first Black president.

Jindal was expected to argue that Obama’s economic program—particularly the recently enacted $787 billion stimulus package—relied too heavily on federal spending and debt. He advocated tax relief, restrained government and state-level innovation instead.

### Biography

Born Piyush Jindal in Baton Rouge in 1971, Jindal is the son of immigrants from India. He adopted the nickname “Bobby” as a child and converted from Hinduism to Roman Catholicism while in high school.

He graduated from Brown University and studied at Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar. His early career centered on health policy and public administration. At 24, he was appointed secretary of Louisiana’s Department of Health and Hospitals, where he earned attention for efforts to control the agency’s budget. He later led the University of Louisiana System and served in President George W. Bush’s administration as an assistant secretary at the Department of Health and Human Services.

### Political rise and record

Jindal narrowly lost the 2003 Louisiana governor’s race but won a seat in the U.S. House the following year. He was reelected in 2006 before running again for governor in 2007, winning outright and avoiding a runoff. At 36, he became the nation’s youngest sitting governor and the first Indian American elected governor of a U.S. state.

As governor, Jindal emphasized:

- Stronger ethics and financial-disclosure rules for state officials;
- Tax cuts and measures intended to improve Louisiana’s business climate;
- Government restructuring and tighter spending controls;
- Education and workforce-development initiatives;
- Disaster preparedness, particularly during Hurricane Gustav in 2008.

His handling of Gustav enhanced his national reputation. Rather than attend the Republican National Convention, Jindal remained in Louisiana to oversee the storm response, drawing favorable comparisons with the government’s widely criticized handling of Hurricane Katrina three years earlier.

### Presidential speculation

The rebuttal assignment immediately intensified speculation that Jindal could seek the Republican presidential nomination in 2012. At 37, he offered the party a youthful, policy-oriented profile, executive experience and a compelling family story. He had also developed relationships with national Republican donors and activists and had campaigned for GOP candidates around the country.

Jindal said he was focused on governing Louisiana and dismissed talk of an imminent presidential campaign. Nevertheless, being chosen for the high-profile response effectively placed him on the party’s national stage and made him a plausible future contender.

The assignment carried risks as well as opportunities: opposition responses are difficult to deliver, and Jindal would be speaking immediately after a popular new president during a severe economic crisis. Still, the selection made clear that Republican leaders viewed him as an important representative of the party’s next generation.

## Jindal steps onto national stage with GOP response to Obama

**WASHINGTON —** Louisiana Gov. Bobby Jindal assumed one of the Republican Party’s most visible roles Tuesday night, delivering the party’s response to President Barack Obama and presenting himself as a leading voice in the GOP’s effort to rebuild after its 2008 election losses.

Jindal, then 37, used the nationally televised address following Obama’s speech to Congress on February 24, 2009, to challenge the president’s economic agenda. He argued that Republicans favored tax relief, restrained federal spending and greater state and local control rather than the expansive federal programs promoted by the new administration.

The assignment immediately intensified attention on Jindal as a possible contender for the 2012 Republican presidential nomination. Although he had said he was focused on governing Louisiana, party officials regarded him as part of a younger generation that could broaden the GOP’s appeal.

### Louisiana record

Jindal was elected governor in 2007 after serving in the U.S. House of Representatives and holding senior state and federal health-policy positions. He entered office promising to overhaul Louisiana’s political culture, strengthen ethics laws and improve a state government still struggling with the consequences of Hurricanes Katrina and Rita.

His supporters pointed to ethics legislation, economic-development initiatives and efforts to streamline government as evidence that he could translate conservative ideas into policy. His administration also emphasized hurricane preparedness and emergency management—subjects Jindal highlighted in his response to Obama by recalling his experience during Hurricane Katrina and criticizing bureaucratic failures.

Critics, however, questioned parts of his budget strategy and argued that some of his reform claims were overstated. His decision to oppose portions of the federal economic stimulus package also placed him at the center of a broader debate among Republican governors over whether ideological opposition should outweigh the immediate needs of recession-stricken states.

### A prominent Indian-American Republican

Born Piyush Jindal in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, to immigrants from India, Jindal adopted the nickname “Bobby” as a child. Raised in a Hindu household, he converted to Roman Catholicism as a teenager.

His rise carried historic significance. He became the first Indian-American elected governor of a U.S. state and, at the time, one of the country’s most prominent Indian-American officeholders. His background gave Republicans an opportunity to showcase greater diversity at a moment when the party was trying to recover support among younger voters and minority communities.

Jindal generally resisted being defined primarily by ethnicity, emphasizing his identity as an American and a Louisianan. Still, his family’s immigrant story featured prominently in his national introduction and reinforced his party’s message about opportunity and upward mobility.

### Role in McCain’s campaign

During the 2008 presidential race, Jindal emerged as an energetic surrogate for Republican nominee John McCain. He campaigned on McCain’s behalf, defended the Arizona senator’s policies and was mentioned during the vice-presidential selection process, although McCain ultimately chose Alaska Gov. Sarah Palin.

Jindal’s participation in the campaign helped him develop relationships with national Republican donors, strategists and activists. It also raised his profile beyond Louisiana, positioning him as a potential spokesman on health care, fiscal policy and government reform.

After McCain’s defeat, Republicans began debating how to respond to Obama’s popularity and the Democratic Party’s control of Washington. Jindal’s selection to answer Obama suggested that GOP leaders saw him as an important part of that response.

### Questions about 2012

The speaking assignment inevitably fueled presidential speculation. Jindal’s age, biography and conservative credentials made him an attractive prospect to some Republicans searching for a candidate who could represent generational change.

But a presidential campaign would have carried risks. Jindal was still early in his first term as governor, and he repeatedly said his priority was Louisiana. A national campaign also would have subjected his state record and policy positions to far more scrutiny.

His televised performance received mixed—and often sharply negative—reviews. Some Republican commentators criticized its delivery as overly slow and awkward, underscoring how difficult it can be to respond to a president speaking before a joint session of Congress. The reaction complicated what had been intended as a major national debut, though it did not remove Jindal from discussions about the party’s future.

Whether or not he pursued the presidency in 2012, the address established Jindal as a national Republican figure. It also gave him the difficult task of defining a conservative alternative to a popular new president during an economic crisis—a challenge that would shape the Republican Party in the years ahead.
